s18.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 4:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — USA–CANADA
body: The sun at twenty to five comes in level off the Channel and straight through the Fishbowl’s glass, and from the lobby the lounge is a tank of gold with people in it: the backs of heads over the couch, steam off somebody’s cocoa, Doug Pruitt on his feet in front of the television with his hand over his heart. The anthem is coming out of five speakers he carried down from 420 himself.
At the foot of the stairs Jack makes his pitch with one hand on the rail. “Theo’s MacBook is upstairs. Four-twelve. Two people and a laptop, and no chanting.”

Skye is already turning toward the glass. “I’ve been in a motel with a horse for two weeks,” she says. “I want a *room*.” She has the door open while he’s still standing there holding the plan, and the anthem comes out at them across the carpet with all its brass, and she pulls him in by the sleeve of the Carhartt, past Priya’s laminate on the glass.

The Logitech has been liberated from 420 for the duration and wired in under the TV cart, the subwoofer squatting on the carpet like a footlocker, the speaker wire taped down in long silver stripes. Taped to the cart, at Doug’s eye level:

body.title: Taped to the TV cart, the Fishbowl
body.text:
TEMPORARY A/V INSTALLATION — APPROVED
For the duration of the XXI Olympic Winter Games ONLY.
All wire to be taped DOWN.
— P. Raman, RA, 4th floor
(Doug: this means the subwoofer too.)

body: The anthem ends. Doug takes his hand off his heart and starts in under his breath, through his teeth, on a technicality: “U. S. A. U. S. A.” Priya looks up from her table by the door. He goes on mouthing it.

Forty-one seconds after the puck drops, an American defenseman named Rafalski puts one in from the point, and the Fishbowl goes up. Doug is standing on the couch cushions with both arms in the air. Priya stands to object, finds that the Handbook has nothing on this, and sits back down.
Theo has the near end of the couch, loafers crossed on the coffee table, the only man in the room betting against his own country. “I have a burrito on Canada,” he tells them. “On principle.”
“What principle?” says Skye.
“Universal health care and a better class of apology.” He looks up at her from under his eyebrows. “Callender.”
“Ted.”

Yusuf, cross-legged on the carpet at Theo’s feet, holds the other end of the burrito and has written the terms on the back of his hand in ballpoint. Kevin and Clare have the loveseat. Clare is in a Sharks cap, explaining icing to Doug for the third time, now with a napkin for the rink and a sugar packet for the puck; one of her four brothers plays club, and she’s been explaining icing to boys since she could talk.
“So it’s like offsides,” Doug says.
“It is not like offsides.”
“It’s like *diet* offsides.”
Margot has the armchair and a thesis. “It’s a cold war,” she says, “fought by dentists’ sons.”

And at the far table under the window, where the gold comes in strongest, Laney has her boots up on a second chair and Lena has a paperback flat under one hand and a pencil in the other. She has read straight through the anthem.

Skye does the room. She goes around it in order, the way she does everything when she’s glad: Margot first, who allows herself to be hugged in the armchair with her arms at her sides; Kevin, who stands up to be hugged and then doesn’t know when to sit down; Clare, who says *Oh!* and hugs back hard; Doug from behind, which makes him yell. She doesn’t let go of Jack’s hand for any of it, so he goes too, around the couch and past the TV cart, toward the window.

As they come past the far table Lena looks up from the book. “Welcome back,” she says to Skye — her mother’s manners, Mémère’s maybe, warm enough to be real — and Skye says, “Thank you. It’s good to be back,” and Lena’s eyes go down to the page again, and the pencil moves. Not one word to Jack. Not a look he could prove.

It was courteous, every syllable of it, and it was for Skye, and it was the right thing to say to a girl home from two weeks away. Jack is at the pop machine by the door with a dollar half into the slot and no memory of the carpet in between. The machine takes the dollar, thinks it over, and gives it back.
From the far table Laney calls across the room, all honey, “Skye, darlin’, you look like a whole Western,” and Skye touches the brim of a hat she isn’t wearing.

Then Laney is at his elbow. Doug’s Igloo sits on the carpet beside the machine, full of ice and not much else, and she bends to it and goes through the ice with her bare hand, choosing the last Diet Coke as if it had wronged her. When she speaks it’s the first thing she has said out loud to him since the curb, and she says it low, so it carries exactly as far as he is.

body.text: “Careful with the coffee table, fireman. Things slide.”

body: She straightens up with the can, and she’s back at the far table with her boots on the chair before he has anything.
On the loveseat Clare has turned right around to Kevin and is thanking him in front of the room:

body.text: “Thank you for the roses. You signed it *Kevin*. Just Kevin. I liked that.”
“Thank you for the strings. Nobody has ever got the gauge right. Not even my grandfather.”
“Thank you for the letter.” She lets that go by a moment. “I’ve read it more than once.”
“My brothers told me they voted. Thank you for the jersey. And the chocolates. Javi says the chocolates were the minority report.”

body: Kevin looks at the floor, and once, across the room, at Jack, and back down at the floor.
“Dude,” Doug says, with the Igloo’s lid up. “We’re *out*. Who’s got legs?”

Skye has her coat over her arm and is standing in the middle of the carpet looking for where the two of them go. There’s the orange chair by the door, with its back to the glass and a cigarette burn in one arm from some year before Priya. There’s the middle of the couch, where Theo has moved his loafers over to make a place, dead in front of the screen with the window just past it. “There,” Skye says, and points at the couch.

response: He takes the orange chair by the door instead. Skye follows him over and sits on the arm of it with her boots in his lap and the sheepskin over the both of them. She doesn’t say a word about the couch. From here the screen is a little sideways and the whole room is between him and the window, and he can see every bit of the game he needs to.

choices.text: *The middle of the couch, where Skye wants it.*
response: The middle of the couch, then. Skye tucks in against him under the sheepskin like it’s a blanket at a drive-in, her dark head on his shoulder, Theo’s loafers back up on the coffee table on one side and Margot’s armchair on the other. The screen is dead ahead. Just past its left edge, under the window, is the far table, and a pencil moving at it. He watches the game harder than anybody has ever watched hockey. By the end of the period he understands icing.

choices.text: *Volunteer for a pop run and take the long way.*
response: “I’ll go.” He takes orders. Doug: “Mountain Dew, dude, it’s *patriotic*.” Theo, a ginger ale, “in a glass bottle, if Delgado has evolved.” Skye, root beer. He takes the long way, down through the basement and past the laundry, the sweet chemical heat of it and the dryer at the end of the row standing open with nobody’s sweatshirt in it, to the machine by the boiler room that still takes dollars.

He comes back up with his arms full of cans to find the room on its feet again. He has missed Rafalski’s second. Doug narrates it to him in full, on the coffee table, with the cans: the Mountain Dew is Rafalski, the ginger ale is the Canadian goalie, and the root beer, tragically, is the puck.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Wednesday they were all in 412 when I came back for my jacket: her birthday, she said; Kevin said the fourteenth, Valentine’s. A party for her on Bacchus Sunday, at the Broussards’. Friday at the curb: “Have a nice weekend, fireman.” Presidents’ Day night she came through the lobby in sunglasses with four bags, said happy birthday to Kevin, and went past me. Sunday at the hockey she told Skye she looks like a whole Western. At the cooler she told me: careful with the coffee table, fireman. Things slide.

journal.title: Clare Dominguez
journal.text: Clare Dominguez. Newman sophomore. Plays violin in the Mass band. Played ‘Ashokan Farewell’ at the Haiti table and people stopped on the lawn. Kevin’s mother knows her mother. Everybody’s mother knows her mother. Four brothers, back in San Jose. Knows football better than Kevin. Wore a 49ers cap to Sully’s. At the Walk for Life a man with a megaphone screamed at her, and she kept praying. Skye stood in front of her. Sunday in the Fishbowl, USA–Canada: one of her brothers plays club hockey, and she explained icing to Doug three times. She thanked Kevin for what came on Valentine’s: red roses, the card in his hand.

s18a.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 6:30 PM · THE FISHBOWL — THE THIRD PERIOD
body: At the second intermission the far table empties. Lena closes the paperback on the pencil and puts it under her arm, and Laney stands and slides her arm through Lena’s, and they go.

body.text: They go out past his chair, close enough that Lena’s cardigan sleeve all but brushes his knee, and Laney’s perfume comes after them, something with vanilla in it. They don’t slow. He watches the Zamboni on the screen going around on the clean ice until the glass door has swung shut behind them.

He doesn’t see them go. He knows they’ve gone because the sightline has: the far table is just a table at the edge of the screen, two empty chairs and a wet ring on the Formica where a can stood, and his shoulders come down an inch he didn’t know they were up.

He’s on cans again by then, by acclamation, and he meets them on the basement stairs coming up with his arms full. Laney says, “Oh, look. Room service,” to the stairwell at large. Lena says nothing, and goes up on the far side of the rail.

body: The third period belongs to the American goalie. His name is Miller, and he stands in his crease in Vancouver and gets shot at by the entire nation of Canada from every angle there is, and stops it, and stops it. Yusuf, on the carpet, has started counting the saves out loud without anybody asking him to, carrying the total over from the first two periods. “Thirty-eight,” he says, to no one. “Thirty-nine.” Theo, whose burrito is going down with every number, asks him to stop. “Forty.”

Late, Canada gets one back, and the room goes so quiet that the subwoofer is the loudest thing in it: the crowd in Vancouver coming up through the carpet like weather. Clare has both hands over her mouth. Kevin has a thumbnail in his teeth. By the door Priya has risen to her feet and doesn’t seem to know it. “Forty-one,” says Yusuf. “Forty-two.”

With under a minute left Canada pulls its goalie for the extra man, and the net at the far end of the ice stands empty, and an American named Kesler chases down a loose puck and puts it in the empty net, and that’s the game. USA 5, Canada 3.

The Fishbowl goes up. Doug is on the arm of the couch, which is against the Handbook, with his arms straight up like a referee. Priya’s laminate has come unstuck from the glass in the uproar and slid down onto the carpet, and Priya isn’t picking it up. Clare is pounding Kevin on the shoulder with her fist, and Kevin is letting her. Theo stands and pays Yusuf a burrito with a ten-dollar bill and dignity. Margot remarks that nobody has asked her opinion.

Jack is on his feet with the rest of them, yelling at a hockey game, a sport he did not know the rules of at four o’clock. Skye comes up on her toes in front of him and takes his face in both her hands and kisses him, hard, laughing into it, in the middle of the carpet with Doug’s chant coming down on them from the arm of the couch. Then she ducks her head and puts it under his chin, the dark hair, no hat, still smelling of motel shampoo, and he gets both arms around her and the sheepskin and lifts her a little off the floor, and he’s happy, all at once and at the top of his voice, with a hockey game going and her mouth tasting of Swiss Miss.

Over her head he watches Priya pick her laminate up off the carpet, read it, and lay it on her table, words down. Doug starts the chant again from the arm of the couch, and the room takes it up, and somewhere in it, under her breath, so does Priya.

s19.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 8:30 PM · THE ANCHOR — THE BACK BOOTH
body: Sunday night at the Anchor is three fishermen at the counter with their caps on, the jukebox dark, and Rudy’s transistor on the shelf over the flattop with a ballgame on it in Spanish, a crowd the size of a thumbnail going up and coming down. On a Sunday Jack comes in the front door like a customer, and from this side of the pass the kitchen looks smaller.

He asked them in the lobby after the game, one at a time, by name: Theo, Kevin, Margot. Clare had quartet. So it’s the five of them in the back booth, Skye on the inside against the window and Jack on the outside with his knee against hers under the table, and the front door in the corner of his eye.
Gloria arrives with the menus under her arm and the pencil out of her hair, and stops at the end of the booth with her weight on one hip, and gives Skye a good long look.

body.text: “The peach,” she says. “You owe me a verdict on the lattice.”
body.else: “So you’re why I gave him Saturday,” she says.

body: The chalkboard over the pie case says APPLE — LATTICE in Gloria’s capitals. She brings a slice before anybody has ordered one and sets it down in front of Skye with the fork standing up in it.

Skye sits up for it. She cuts a corner with the side of the fork, looks at the cross-hatching, eats it slowly with her eyes shut, and opens them on Gloria. “Pretty on top,” she says. “Everything’s leaking underneath.”
Gloria puts the pencil behind her ear and turns to Jack, delighted. “That’s what I said about *him*.”
Skye looks at Jack. Jack looks at the pie. He rates it a seven, to change the subject, and Gloria says that’s generous from a man with his record, and goes for the coffee.

Theo and Skye are doing Los Angeles across the table at each other. Debbie threw the crew a party in the motel courtyard on the last night, with a rented chocolate fountain that froze solid at seven thousand feet and had to be served with a chisel. Theo counters with his mother, who once threw a party to apologize for a party.
“Two women,” Theo says, “who throw parties as policy.”
“Foreign policy,” says Skye.
“Domestic. It’s worse.”
Margot has her notebook out and is interviewing Skye about Dell for what she calls a footnote. “Is she likable?”
“God, no.”
“Does she smile?”
“Once. At the horse. Ana cut it.”
Margot writes that down. “A woman who refuses likability is a political act.”
Skye points her fork at her across the table. “She just doesn’t like her dad’s questions.”

Kevin is eating his coffee cake carefully, the way he has done everything since the Fishbowl, as if it might be taken back. “Clare asked me to come hear her play next Sunday, at the five-thirty,” he says, cutting a corner off. “I go anyway. She asked anyway.” He looks over at Jack and then down at his fork again, and he’s smiling at the fork.

Jack catches Theo watching him. Theo has his cup halfway up and is looking across the booth at Jack with Skye’s head on his shoulder and her boot hooked around his ankle under the table, and he keeps looking, long enough that Jack sees him see it. Then he sets the cup down in its saucer.
“Kevin,” Theo says. “Picture it. The Newman spring retreat. A silent one. At a vineyard.”
“Respectfully, no.”
“Silence, Tran. Grapes. A sommelier who has taken a vow.”

Margot says she would attend a silent retreat only as an ethnographer. Skye says she’ll go if there’s a horse. Kevin says there will be no horse, and no vineyard, and no retreat, and Theo writes VINEYARD on a napkin and puts it in his breast pocket, where Jack has seen a lot of ideas go to wait.
Gloria comes back with the pot and fills Skye’s cup first, and stands there with it to tell her the hair is a crime and it suits her.
“It washes out,” Skye says. “Twelve washes.”
“Don’t hurry it, hon.”

In the lot after, Skye has the Saab running for the heater and both hands on the wheel, and she doesn’t put it in gear. Through the windshield the Anchor’s front window is yellow, and inside it Gloria is putting the chairs up on the tables, one by one, legs in the air. Skye watches her do three of them.
“You’ve been arranging rooms all day, Youngstown.”

body.text: “Four-twelve, with a laptop. Then the chair by the door. Then this booth, with the door on your side.”
“Four-twelve, with a laptop. Then you sat in the middle of that couch like it was going to bite you.”
“Four-twelve, with a laptop. Then a pop run through the *basement*. Then this booth, with the door on your side.”

body: She says it easily, with her head back against the rest and the dash lights green along the side of her face, and her eyes on him, and then she waits.

choices.key: When Skye said you’d been arranging rooms all day, you told her Laney’s mad at you.
response: It’s true. It isn’t all of it.

“Laney’s mad at you *loudly*,” Skye says. She turns that over and seems to find it the right size. “Okay.” She puts the Saab in reverse, one arm across the back of his seat, looking out the rear window past his ear, and backs them out under the light.

choices.key: When Skye said you’d been arranging rooms all day, you told her you wanted her to yourself.
response: She takes it. She leans across the gearshift and kisses him, slow, with the engine going and the heater blowing on their knees, and when she sits back she’s smiling, and whatever else there is stays outside in the lot with the dumpster and the gulls.

choices.text: “Theo taught me seating. It’s a sickness.”
response: She laughs, with her head back against the rest, a real laugh that fogs a little patch of the windshield. She looks over at him. “That’s a good line,” she says. “That’s not an answer.” And she puts it in first and drives.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’ Thursday I asked her for Saturday night. ‘Who’s she?’ ‘You met her.’ ‘Boysenberry.’ She gave it to Rudy’s nephew. Her granddaughter got her watching *Sweetwater*; Thursdays at nine, for the clothes. She rated Cassidy a vanilla custard. Skye agreed. Tuesday morning she had the day girl’s shift. Hale sat in our booth till two Sunday morning reading her Housman; she put him in a cab. Theo pitched me New Orleans on her placemats. She rated it a meringue: all air, and it still costs four dollars. She gave me Saturday the twentieth off. Go get your peach; Rudy’ll cover the Hobart. Rudy said no. Sunday night the peach rated her lattice: pretty on top, everything leaking underneath. Gloria said that’s what she said about me.
